strengths: First work to combine architecture-agnostic Graph Meta-Networks with representation learning for NeRFs, addressing a real limitation of prior methods (nf2vec, tri-plane processing) that are locked to a single architecture.

Clear and well-motivated combination of a rendering loss with a SigLIP-style contrastive loss, with a thoughtful ablation (LR, LR+C, LC) that reveals complementary trade-offs between class separability and architecture invariance.

Thorough experimental protocol covering both single- and multi-architecture settings, classification and retrieval tasks, and generalization to six unseen architectural variants (different depths, widths, grid resolutions, channel counts), which is a meaningful robustness test.
Good qualitative analysis via t-SNE visualizations that intuitively explain why LR alone fails to unify architectures and how the contrastive loss helps.

Method matches or beats prior single-architecture baselines (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) in the single-architecture setting despite being more general, which strengthens the practical value of the approach.
Reasonably detailed appendix with implementation/training details supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to only two NeRF architectures (MLP and tri-plane) from prior work, both explicitly acknowledged as not state-of-the-art; no experiments with hash-grid-based NeRFs (Instant-NGP) or voxel-based NeRFs, which are the most commonly used in practice, limiting the claim of true architecture-agnosticism.

Dataset is limited to synthetic ShapeNetRender objects with relatively small MLPs (3 layers, dim 64) and small tri-planes (32x32x16); scalability to larger, more realistic/real-world NeRFs is untested.

Instance-level retrieval performance is quite low (recall@1 around 29-45%), and the paper somewhat downplays this by pointing to qualitative similarity in nearest neighbors rather than proposing ways to improve it.

The three loss variants (LR, LR+C, LC) show inconsistent best performers across tasks/settings, and there is no single recommended configuration or principled way to select λ beyond matching loss magnitudes; this weakens the practical takeaway of the paper.

Training cost is very high (2 weeks on a single RTX 3090 for LR/LR+C), and no computational comparison to baselines (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) is given, raising concerns about efficiency of the GMN-based approach.
No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance analysis are reported for any of the classification/retrieval numbers, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported gains.

The paper does not report results for the actual GMN with unseen architectures class recall in Table 2 comparisons methods marked with dashes (e.g., nf2vec, Cardace et al. rows are often empty '—'), which makes some tables slightly confusing/less informative as direct comparisons.

Limited novelty in the technical components themselves (GMN from Lim et al. 2024, decoder from nf2vec, SigLIP loss from Zhai et al. 2023); the contribution is primarily a combination/application rather than a new architecture or loss.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically relevant limitation of prior NeRF meta-network methods (nf2vec, Cardace et al.), which are locked to a single predefined architecture.

Well-designed ablation isolating the effect of rendering loss vs. contrastive (SigLIP) loss, supported by clear and convincing t-SNE visualizations that explain why a rendering loss alone fails to align different architectures in latent space.
Reasonably comprehensive experimental matrix covering classification and both instance-level and class-level retrieval, in both single- and multi-architecture settings.
Attempts to test generalization to architectures not seen during training (varying depth/width/resolution), which is a relevant and interesting question for meta-network research.
Clear writing and good contextualization within the meta-network and contrastive-learning literature.
weaknesses: The central claim of being 'architecture-agnostic' for 'arbitrary NeRF architectures' is overstated: experiments are confined to only two architecture families (a plain MLP and a tri-plane+MLP), both from prior work and explicitly acknowledged by the authors as 'not state-of-the-art.' No hash-grid (Instant-NGP/Zip-NeRF) or voxel-grid NeRFs are tested, which are far more common in practice and would be a much stronger test of the architecture-agnostic claim.

The so-called 'unseen architectures' (MLP-2L, MLP-32H, TRI-2L, TRI-32H, TRI-16W, TRI-8C) are merely hyperparameter variants of the same two architecture families seen at training time, not structurally novel/unseen architectures. This significantly weakens the paper's headline contribution of generalizing to unseen architectures.

Instance-level retrieval—the task that most directly demonstrates the value of an architecture-agnostic embedding—performs quite poorly (recall@1 in the 29–45% range even for the best variant), undermining the practical usefulness of the proposed embedding space for the very task it is designed to enable.

No comparison against simple, non-weight-based baselines (e.g., rendering a few views and using an off-the-shelf image encoder), which the introduction dismisses on efficiency grounds but never empirically evaluates; such a baseline would help contextualize whether the added complexity of the GMN approach is justified.

Results are inconsistent across loss variants (LR best for some settings, LC best for others, LR+C a compromise), and there is no single configuration that is clearly superior, making the practical takeaway for a user unclear; no guidance/criterion is given for choosing among the three variants at deployment time.

Training cost is very high (~2 weeks on a single GPU for LR/LR+C), which is not discussed as a limitation and raises reproducibility/scalability concerns given the modest scale of the two-architecture experiments.
Experiments rely on a single dataset source (ShapeNetRender-derived NeRFs, 13 synthetic classes), limiting evidence for generalization to real-world scenes or more diverse object categories.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance testing are reported for any of the numerical results, making it hard to assess whether observed differences (e.g., between LR, LR+C, LC) are robust or within noise.

The technical contribution is largely a combination of existing components (GMN encoder from Lim et al., nf2vec decoder, SigLIP loss from Zhai et al.), with relatively modest novel methodological content beyond this combination.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important limitation of prior NeRF-weight-processing methods (nf2vec, Cardace et al.), which are locked to a single, fixed architecture; this paper is the first to demonstrate architecture-agnostic processing of NeRF weights, including generalization to architectures unseen at training time.

The combination of a rendering loss with a SigLIP-style contrastive loss is well motivated and empirically justified: the t-SNE analysis in Section 4.1/Figure 3 clearly shows how LR alone creates architecture-specific sub-clusters, while LC and LR+C progressively unify architectures into shared, class-organized clusters, giving a clear mechanistic explanation for the design choice.

Fairly comprehensive experimental protocol covering both single- and multi-architecture settings, classification and (instance- and class-level) retrieval tasks, and a dedicated study of generalization to six unseen architecture variants (depth, width, spatial resolution, channel count).

Where a direct comparison is possible (single-architecture setting), the proposed method matches or slightly exceeds specialized baselines (nf2vec, Cardace et al.), suggesting the added flexibility does not come at a cost in the settings those baselines can handle.

Reasonably detailed appendix with dataset, architecture and training hyperparameter descriptions, and additional qualitative/quantitative results (class-level retrieval, extended t-SNE, retrieval visualizations), which aids reproducibility given the codebases are built on existing public implementations.
weaknesses: Experimental validation is confined to only two closely related NeRF architecture families (a small MLP and a tri-plane+small MLP), both non-state-of-the-art as the authors themselves admit; the "unseen architecture" experiments only vary width/depth/resolution within the same family rather than testing structurally different designs (e.g., hash-grid/Instant-NGP, voxel grids), which weakens the claim of true architecture-agnosticism implied by the title ("Any NeRF").

No baseline is provided for a simpler alternative such as training separate single-architecture encoders (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) and post-hoc aligning their embedding spaces (e.g., via Procrustes/CCA or a lightweight adapter); such a baseline would help isolate how much benefit comes specifically from the joint GMN encoder versus simpler alignment strategies.

Absolute performance on the core new capability (instance-level cross-architecture retrieval) is modest, e.g., 29-45% recall@1, indicating the problem is far from solved despite the architecture-agnostic framing; this is acknowledged but somewhat undercuts the practical significance of the contribution.

Reported results appear to be single-run numbers without variance/multiple seeds, and training is very expensive (~2 weeks per configuration on a single RTX 3090), which limits confidence in the robustness of comparisons and reproducibility for others without similar compute.

The technical contribution is largely a combination of existing components (GMN from Lim et al., nf2vec decoder from Zama Ramirez et al., SigLIP loss from Zhai et al.) applied to a new but narrow experimental setting, so novelty is more in problem framing/application than in new methodology.

Many baseline cells in the tables are "—" because prior methods are architecturally incapable of running in the multi-architecture setting; while expected, this means several of the paper's central comparisons are against nothing rather than empirically outperforming a competing approach, somewhat limiting the strength of the comparative evidence.

strengths: First framework to process NeRFs of diverse architectures (MLPs, tri-planes, hash tables) with a single architecture-agnostic encoder, extending GMNs to a novel and practically relevant setting.

Novel parameter-graph construction for multi-resolution hash tables that avoids cubic scaling with grid resolution, a meaningful technical contribution beyond prior GMN work which only handled linear layers and tri-planes.

Thorough ablation of loss objectives (rendering-only, contrastive-only, combined) with clear qualitative (t-SNE) and quantitative evidence explaining the complementary roles of each loss in shaping the latent space.

Extensive experimental matrix: 13 architectures across 3 families, both single- and multi-architecture settings, seen and unseen architectures, classification and retrieval tasks, plus cross-dataset generalization to Objaverse-trained NeRFs.
Method matches or exceeds prior architecture-specific baselines (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) even in their own single-architecture setting, showing the generalization does not come at a significant cost.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendices on graph construction, training hyperparameters, dataset architectures, and hardware/implementation details.
weaknesses: All experiments (aside from one qualitative generalization test) rely on a single dataset, ShapenetRender, with synthetic objects of limited diversity; this restricts confidence in broader applicability, as acknowledged by the authors themselves.

Retrieval performance (Table 6) is fairly low in absolute terms (e.g., Recall@1 around 30% even for LR+C in several settings), and the paper leans heavily on qualitative figures to argue that the method still captures meaningful semantic similarity despite low quantitative recall — this argument is somewhat hand-wavy and could be strengthened with more rigorous analysis or additional metrics.

The single fixed choice of λ=2e-2 for balancing the rendering and contrastive losses is under-motivated (chosen so the two loss magnitudes are similar) and no sensitivity analysis or ablation over λ is provided, leaving open whether the observed trade-offs are an artifact of this specific weighting.

Performance on unseen architectures within a family can degrade dramatically in certain cases (e.g., TRI-16W, HASH-11T, and cross-family generalization), and while the paper notes these as directions for future work, the underlying causes are not analyzed in depth (e.g., why hash table size changes are so disruptive).

The architectural novelty is somewhat incremental: the encoder (GMN from Lim et al.) and decoder (nf2vec) are both taken directly from prior work, with the main technical novelty being the hash-table graph conversion and the application of a SigLIP-style contrastive loss; the conceptual leap, while useful, is not deeply novel in isolation.

No comparison to simpler or alternative architecture-agnostic baselines (e.g., a naive concatenation/flattening-based encoder trained across architectures with padding, or a shared MLP with architecture-conditioning) to justify that a full GMN treatment is necessary versus simpler alternatives.

The paper does not report computational cost/efficiency trade-offs versus prior single-architecture methods, despite the additional overhead of graph construction and message passing, which could matter for practical adoption.

strengths: First framework demonstrated to process NeRFs of genuinely diverse architectures (MLP, tri-plane, hash table) via a graph meta-network, with a novel and memory-efficient parameter-graph construction for multi-resolution hash tables that is a real technical contribution beyond Lim et al.

Thorough ablation of loss objectives (rendering-only, contrastive-only, combined) with an insightful latent-space (t-SNE) analysis that explains why rendering loss alone clusters by architecture rather than content, motivating the addition of a SigLIP-style contrastive term

Experiments span 13 architectures across 3 families and cover both classification and retrieval, including a stress test on architectures unseen at training time and a qualitative generalization test to an out-of-distribution dataset (Objaverse)

In the single-architecture setting the proposed encoder matches or exceeds prior specialized baselines (nf2vec, Cardace et al.), suggesting the more general framework does not sacrifice performance on the original narrow use case
Reasonably detailed appendix with implementation/training details and additional qualitative figures that aid reproducibility
weaknesses: All NeRFs (aside from one qualitative generalization test) are trained on a single dataset (ShapeNetRender); architectural diversity is high but scene/content diversity is essentially absent, which is a significant limitation for claims of general-purpose 'weight-space representation learning' and is only acknowledged post-hoc as future work

Generalization to 'unseen' architectures is fairly narrow (mostly changes in hidden dim/layers/resolution within the same family) rather than truly novel architectural designs; results are also quite inconsistent (e.g., TRI-16W and HASH-11T accuracies drop to near-chance or the 20-30% range), undermining the headline claim of robust architecture-agnostic generalization

Retrieval performance in absolute terms is weak, especially recall@1 (often <15-30%) and the ALL/ALL setting with LR collapses to ~0%, indicating the architecture-agnostic latent space is far from reliable for fine-grained instance retrieval

The rendering vs. contrastive loss trade-off is not resolved: users must choose a checkpoint (LR vs LR+C vs LC) depending on the downstream task, which weakens the claimed unified 'architecture-agnostic' embedding and complicates practical deployment

Novelty is somewhat incremental: encoder (GMN from Lim et al.), decoder (nf2vec), and contrastive loss (SigLIP) are all borrowed directly from prior work; the core new contribution is essentially the hash-table graph conversion

Comparisons to baselines are frequently unavailable ('–' entries) because nf2vec/Cardace et al. cannot handle most settings, so many of the 'superiority' claims rest on comparisons against no real competing method rather than a genuinely controlled baseline
No naive render-then-classify baseline is reported, which would help calibrate how much value the weight-space approach actually provides over simpler alternatives

Scalability/cost of the GMN approach for larger or more complex hash tables/scenes is not discussed, and training times reported (~2 weeks per configuration) raise practical concerns for a framework intended to generalize across many architectures

strengths: Addresses a genuine and significant limitation of prior NeRF weight-space processing frameworks (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) that are restricted to a single, fixed architecture; the proposed framework is the first to handle multiple, diverse NeRF architectures within a unified latent space.

Novel and memory-efficient parameter-graph construction for multi-resolution hash tables, extending the GMN formulation of Lim et al. to a previously unaddressed and now widely-used NeRF architecture family.

Thorough empirical analysis of the interplay between rendering and contrastive losses, including an insightful t-SNE study that clearly demonstrates why a rendering loss alone fails to produce an architecture-agnostic latent space and motivates the addition of the SigLIP-style contrastive term.

Broad experimental coverage: 13 architectures across three families, both single- and multi-architecture settings, classification and retrieval tasks, and generalization tests to unseen architectural hyperparameters and to an entirely different dataset (Objaverse).

In the single-architecture setting, the proposed method matches or exceeds prior specialized baselines (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) while also being applicable to hash-table NeRFs, which neither baseline can process.

Extensive supplementary material (additional graph-construction details, extra ablations with LC, qualitative retrieval figures, implementation/hardware details) supports reproducibility and gives a fairly complete picture of the framework's behavior.
weaknesses: All NeRF datasets (MLP, TRI, HASH, and the unseen variants) are trained on ShapeNetRender only; the single cross-dataset test (ObjaNeRF) is qualitative and limited to MLP-architecture queries, so the claimed generalization to truly novel data distributions and architecture families remains only partially validated, a limitation the authors themselves acknowledge.

Generalization to unseen architectures within a family is inconsistent and sometimes drops sharply (e.g., TRI-16W, HASH-11T, hash table size changes), suggesting the architecture-agnostic property is fairly fragile outside the specific hyperparameter ranges seen at training time.

The three architecture families all still ultimately funnel into a similar MLP backbone with (x,y,z)->(r,g,b,σ) mapping; the framework has not been tested on fundamentally different NeRF designs (e.g., voxel grids, different output formulations, view-dependent color MLPs), so the 'diverse architectures' claim is somewhat narrower than the framing suggests.

Absolute retrieval performance (Recall@k) is fairly low in several cross-architecture query/gallery combinations (e.g., 25-45% Recall@10), and the paper relies heavily on qualitative figures to argue that low recall still reflects meaningful semantic similarity, which is a softer form of evidence.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported for any of the classification/retrieval results, making it hard to assess the robustness of the reported gains, especially where margins between LR and LR+C are small.

The core technical novelty beyond the hash-table graph conversion is largely the application of an existing contrastive objective (SigLIP) to an existing GMN encoder; the methodological contribution is somewhat incremental relative to combining known components (GMN, nf2vec decoder, SigLIP loss).

Comparisons to baselines in the single-architecture setting are mixed rather than uniformly favorable (e.g., Cardace et al. outperforms the proposed method on some unseen tri-plane variants such as TRI-2L/TRI-32H), tempering the claim of 'superior results to previous methods.'

Training cost is high (~2 weeks per model on a single A6000), which may hinder reproducibility and further exploration by other researchers, and this cost/scalability aspect is not discussed as a limitation.
